rv.q: In a performance that made me eager to see her again and again on the stage, Carter gleams with candour and intelligence, yet is also touched by chilliness.
Staunton is magnificent as the titular Mrs Warren, who's bought respectability for her daughter by selling herself.
I did, however, leave unexpectedly entertained, and with further confirmation that they don't make actors as interesting as Staunton anymore.
Staunton and Carter make a wonderful double act, bringing painful emotional truth to the twisting narrative.
Staunton is, as usual, ferociously good, very much the unblushing A Past, breathing fire and feeling into her great speech about the hellish poverty of the class she escaped.
The big scenes between mother and daughter are quietly tremendous, and crackle with a genuine sense of a familial bond without becoming cosy.
It is never staid when Staunton is on stage, though. Both mother and daughter give dignified performances, Staunton the more subtle and formidable with an edge of the dandy.
This latest outing doesn't quite manage to complete a hat-trick of undisputed triumphs, but it is never less than a fascinating evening's theatre.
But if you're hoping for something closer to the bone, you may find this a little too professional.
Fine actress though she is, Staunton struggles to step out of the great man's shadow.

What remains is no radical rethink in either structural or dramatic terms, and for all the reduced running time and the enduring relevance of the play's discussion of gender inequality and capitalist power structures, it still often feels ponderous.
Cooke's slimline text and his lavish production turn a remarkably punchy 130-year old play into exactly what you fear an evening of Bernard Shaw might be: worthy and dull.
Cooke's swift touch direction gently dials up the heat with the gentleness of a paintbrush, but with the momentum of punch to the stomach.
The result is an extraordinary tour de force that brings the play to vivid and compelling life.
Whether it's their existing relationship that gives this production such a charge, or simply that Carter has inherited her mother's gifts, they make a riveting double act.
The result is always keen-eyed and fascinating, as one has long come to expect from Cooke.

Her Mrs Warren is smartly turned out, used to getting her own way... In the last of their several confrontations over just a few moments, she can movingly take us from heartbreak through to anger and exasperation.
Cooke's revival gives us a flavour of what a night out in the West End may have been like a century or more ago... the production is utterly conventional without ever being dull.
Staunton, as the formidable Mrs Kitty Warren, delivers a performance of staggering nuance.

The big selling-point of the show is the casting of Staunton opposite her biological daughter, Bessie Carter, as Vivie. Perhaps the plan was to add layers of emotional depth to the story but the experiment doesn't work.
